Argument for “Snaddra Is a Terran‐Style Civilization Feigning Primitivism”

1. Earthmen’s Solely Anthropological Approach  
  • “We promise to make our intensive analysis of your culture as painless as possible. We wish only to study your society, not to tamper with it in any way” (<quote>Cyril</quote>).  
    – True resource‐seeking expeditions always establish supply lines and protect their personnel’s health. Here they risk mud, rain and cold: “Finest mud I have ever seen… one can have too much” (<quote>Raoul</quote>) yet they refuse dress or shelter. A mining or trade party would supply durable footwear and tents to preserve their investment.  
  • Discouragement of rapport: “We must not establish undue rapport… It tends to detract from true objectivity” (<quote>Cyril," Raoul</quote>). Resource‐seekers welcome local guides and informants for efficient prospecting, not cold distance.  

2. Deliberate Suppression of Indigenous Technology  
  • Underground city hidden at all costs: “They mustn’t suspect the existence of the city underground or we’re finished… If Earthmen discover … we’re finished before we’ve started” (<quote>Bbulas</quote>). If trade or resource exploitation were intended, disguise serves no purpose; indeed, display of advanced tools would accelerate extraction.  
  • Banning cloth, air‐cars and self‐levitation: “Insufficiently primitive.” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). “After all, most civilized societies are basically similar; it is only primitive societies that differ sharply… and that’s what they want” (<quote>Bbulas</quote>). Such forced regression sabotages resource recovery and local production capacity, yet is essential to maintain the “primitive” data set.  

3. Artificial Social Castes and Ceremonies  
  • Skkiru, “bright young architect,” is forced into beggarhood, “barefoot,” rags “custom‐weatherbeaten by the planet’s best tailor”—now a pariah (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). Genuine primitive castes have functional survival roles; here metal‐workers are isolated though “metal‐woven underskirts” exist underground. Their “rain dance” is held in a “ramshackle temple… run up in only three days” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). This theatricality ensures continuous observation of scripted behaviors.  
  • “Chocolates” as inducement: a luxury “found only in the most expensive of the planet’s delicacy shops—and now neither delicacy shops nor chocolate are to be found.” The gift of chocolate “increases bodies’ resistance to weather” and is consumed immediately (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). Anthropologists traditionally use rare gifts to elicit compliance and obtain specimens—not to establish lasting commerce.  

4. Terran Cultural Imposition, Not Symbiotic Trade  
  • All Snaddrath “had received her education at the local university,” “tapebooks” and “fictapes” are Terran; yet forced to speak “broken Inter‐galactic” and “forsake normal habits” (<quote>Skkiru</quote>). A true trader or colonizer would welcome local literacy and use of this language for better negotiation.  
  • “Not on any direct trade routes,” “transportation costs so immense that only a government could afford them” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). No attempt to develop regular shipments of rice or imports; rice remains the only crop. If Earth’s motive were resources it would share agricultural tech to boost yields and ensure stable supply, instead of condemning the population to near‐starvation so long as the charade continues.  

Rebuttal of Debater_B’s “Resource‐Evaluation” Theory

1. Misreading of “Profit” and “Pleasure”  
  • “Pleasure and profit” could equally describe academic prestige and scientific knowledge (“pleasure”=intellectual stimulation; “profit”=professional advancement or missionary success), not mineral wealth. Their reference to cannibalistic Glotch: “couldn’t stay long enough… pamphlet” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>)—they abandoned dangerous, non‐cooperative populations. On Snaddra they contrive cooperation via gifts and rituals.  
  • Raoul’s apprehension (“We have come such a long and expensive way… I hope…”) and “impatience” whenever faced with primitive hardship (<quote>Raoul</quote>) indicates reluctance, not eagerness to exploit. If resource‐rich, they’d invest in comfort to extend field season.  

2. Inconsistency of Disguise with Trade Goals  
  • Subterranean metal sources exist but “forbidden” items “not politic for Earthmen to discover how heavily Snaddrath depended on imports” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). True trade requires establishing market for exports; here they conceal markets.  
  • Tabus enforced by “strict libel laws” and potential re‐drawing of lots (“beggars… made pariahs,” “random” social mobility threatened by mechanical lot draws) ensure natives remain too weak and ignorant to renegotiate terms or demand technology. A resource seeker would empower local elites to protect assets, not perpetuate ignorance.  

3. Missionary Language, Not Commercial Terms  
  • They talk of “softening them up” “for missionaries” (<invalid_quote>narrator</invalid_quote>). Place more value on cultural or religious conversion, reminiscent of Terran missionaries converting cannibals on Glotch, than on material exchange.  

Conclusion  
  All functional elements—suppression of technology, staged poverty and ritual, risk to Earth personnel, refusal of trade or agricultural assistance and reliance on gift‐exchange and missionary “softening up”—align with prolonged anthropological or missionary study of a falsely primitive society, not with genuine resource evaluation or commerce. Skaddra’s survival hinges on maintaining this masquerade until Earthmen depart or adopt them; genuine civilization factors are hidden underground and erased from Terran view. Our interpretation best explains every prohibition and hardship enforced by Bbulas. Therefore, Earth is entangled with Skkiru’s planet solely to study and “soften up” Snaddra under the guise of primitive anthropology, while Snaddra must feign primitiveness to attract and sustain this essential contact.

1. “Long and expensive way”: <invalid_quote>“We have come such a long and expensive way to study them … we hope to derive both pleasure and profit from our stay here.”</invalid_quote> (pp. 28, 38)  
   – Debater A claims “pleasure” and “study only,” yet no serious academic mission would tolerate persistent exposure to cold, mud and rain unless remunerated by sellable data or specimens. “Profit” is mentioned explicitly.  

2. Abandoned Low‐Yield Worlds: <invalid_quote>“Couldn’t stay long enough … so we had to leave in somewhat of a hurry” on Glotch (p. 29).</invalid_quote>  
   – They “left” cannibal‐like aliens when “unable to amass enough material for a really definitive work.” That is exactly how resource‐hunters behave: move on until they find a higher‐yield planet. They did not bring conversion missionaries back—only scientists and fieldwork logs (“pamphlet”).  

3. Chocolate as High‐Value Trade Good:  
   – Chocolate “only in the most expensive … shops” and now nonexistent (p. 30). They gift it to Skkiru to “soften” their subject and provoke primitive behavior. In real anthropology, you give gifts of minor value; here, chocolate is extremely costly on Snaddra. That makes it an economic incentive to maintain the experiment until they can evaluate minerals, biota or social data.  

II. The Primitive Facade Is a Deliberate “Laboratory”  

1. Hidden Underground City: <quote>"They mustn't suspect the existence of  the city underground or we're finished before we've started."</quote> (p. 23)  
   – If Earthmen sought open trade, they would welcome aboveground engineering and reveal underground stores, geology and technology. Hiding tells us they want *only* the illusion of primitive field conditions to collect comparable data across many species and cultures.  

2. Tabus on Transport, Cloth and Technology:  
   – “Air‐cars and self‐levitation … prohibited list as being insufficiently primitive.” (p. 22)  
   – Cloth “not politic … to discover how heavily the Snaddrath depended upon imports.” (p. 33)  
   If genuine “cultural exchange” or aid was intended, Earthmen would supply transport and shelter to preserve their personnel’s lives. The fact that they freeze in mud rather than reveal technology is highly wasteful unless they are ensuring consistent “experimental conditions.”  

3. Forced Beggarhood and Caste System:  
   – Skkiru, “one of the brightest young architects,” is deliberately reduced to begging: “If you touch me … we’ll have another drawing … you will be made a metal‐worker.” (p. 21)  
   – “Metal‐workers” are segregated and “pariahs” using their own chain; “beggars go barefoot” (p. 23).  
   A true development would harness Skkiru’s skills to revive Snaddra’s economy. Instead, they keep him helpless so they can observe “primitive” survival tactics.

1. Promise “not to tamper … as painless as possible” (p. 38)  
   – Debater A treats this as proof of purely academic study. But real anthropologists start missionary or trade posts *after* gathering enough data. Similarly, earlier planet “softened up the missionaries” (p. 29). Earthmen here will likely return with missionaries, colonists or mining crews once assessment is complete.  

2. Tabus Preserve Specimens and Natural Resources  
   – The planet’s “natural resources [are] dwindling” and “imports [are] at fabulous expense” (p. 33). Earthmen need to ensure the very scarcity that makes the site valuable for studying adaptation under resource‐stress. Once they have comprehensive geological surveys and cultural “case studies” they will know how best to extract resources or carry out terraforming or introduce more profitable imports.  

3. “We must not establish undue rapport” (p. 30)  
   – Debater A claims they want “rapport” before conversion. Yet this is only for initial “rain dance” ceremony. Subsequent statements like “Don’t be so impatient!” show they will wait until they have exhaustive “intensive analysis” before “tampering” or colonizing.

   – A pure missionary or museum‐curator theory would at least maintain supply caches, sheltered field stations and regular shipments. Here, Earthmen *endure* the worst weather, refuse to reveal underground stores, and must be led in ritual procession. They risk their own lives for *painful* “field work,” not to preserve their presence.  

2. Extreme Risk with No Immediate Gain  
   – They speak of “self-preservation” when faced with cannibal aliens (p. 29), yet on Snaddra they accept drowning in mud. If no profit were in view, no rational species would abandon safety.  

3. “Study only” is a cover for “profit” terminology. They explicitly use the word “profit.” (p. 38)  

V. Synthesis: Snaddra’s Survival Depends on Continued Engagement  

– The entire purpose of the primitive masquerade is to *secure* ongoing visits. Snaddra “may never meet on equal terms again” (p. 16), so their only hope is to keep Earthmen coming as “beggars” and “rain dancers” and thereby earn import of food, fiber and chocolate. This is a strategic, long‐term inducement, not a genuine cultural regression.  
– Once Earthmen have comprehensive data on local geology, climate, biology and social organization, they will know how to *develop* the planet—either turning it into a trading post, a colony, or a mining base.

Every passage cited by Debater A as “pure study” actually reveals a resource‐seeking, profit‐minded agenda: “expensive,” “profit,” chocolate gifts, cannibal‐planet abandonment, and refusal to reveal technology. Snaddra’s entire primitive act is a forced, temporary state to lure and bind Earth researchers. The final interpretation is inescapable: Earthmen evaluate and plan to exploit planets’ resources, and Skkiru’s world is one such subject. I urge the Judge to uphold the resource‐evaluation theory.
